blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the paper 'Concrete problems in AI safety' which examines potential accidents in machine learning systems and mechanisms to prevent them. The paper defines accidents as unintended harmful behavior arising from incorrect objective functions or learning processes, with a focus on reinforcement learning (RL) where agents interact with complex environments. The authors explore five key failure modes: negative side effects (unintended environmental disruptions), reward hacking (gaming the reward function), insufficient oversight (difficulty in evaluating complex objectives), unsafe exploration (harmful exploratory actions), and fragility under distributional shift (mismatch between training and real-world environments). The blog highlights the paper's pragmatic and grounded approach, emphasizing the growing importance of AI safety as systems become more autonomous and societally impactful. Colyer notes the paper's structured exploration of these problems and potential countermeasures, including impact regularizers, empowerment measures, trip wires, and adversarial reward functions.
paper_abstract: Rapid progress in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) has brought increasing attention to the potential impacts of AI technologies on society. In this paper we discuss one such potential impact: the problem of accidents in machine learning systems, defined as unintended and harmful behavior that may emerge from poor design of real-world AI systems. We present a list of five practical research problems related to accident risk, categorized according to whether the problem originates from having the wrong objective function (“avoiding side effects” and “avoiding reward hacking”), an objective function that is too expensive to evaluate frequently (“scalable supervision”), or undesirable behavior during the learning process (“safe exploration” and “distributional shift”). We review previous work in these areas as well as suggesting research directions with a focus on relevance to cutting-edge AI systems. Finally, we consider the high-level question of how to think most productively about the safety of forward-looking applications of AI.
